about: Serving priors (build.py data.priors, src/model.js priorsFor, node report.js --priors, the --check prior lines and the page's Agents tab): what published work and our own logs already say a many-agent serving run will hit, written down before the run so its result is judged against an expectation. Each row: id, statement, value (a number, a [low, high] range or an object of named numbers), unit, tag, src (a URL or a file with its commit) and applies_when (the recipe facts it needs, all of them; the keys are listed under predicates). A row whose number a run of ours measures later gets a ledger row; the prior stays as the outside reference.

tags.MEASURED-ELSEWHERE: a number someone else published; src is its URL
tags.MEASURED-HERE: our own logged number; src names the file and its commit
tags.INFERRED: arithmetic on the numbers above; it holds until a run measures it

predicates.agent_traffic: the recipe serves coding agents: conditions.workload.kind is the real-agent kind, or it serves at least settings.many_agents_min agents (data/workload.json)
predicates.agents_min: the recipe serves at least this many agents (conditions.workload.agents, else serving.batch)
predicates.moe: the model routes tokens to experts (models.<model>.E above 1)
predicates.layer_split: the model is split by layers over two or more cards (a gpu_split of two or more banks, or the engine's layer_split_re in conditions.engine_flags)
predicates.draft: the recipe has a draft head or MTP (recipe.draft)
predicates.ctx_below: the recipe's context window (recipe.ctx) is below this many tokens

rows.statement: Coding agents served by a prefix-caching engine read 4 to 11 fresh prompt tokens per output token (the coding-agent CLI on SWE-bench: input:output 166-246:1 with cache:new 22-41:1; one vendor model on vLLM automatic prefix caching gives 6.1 and 10.7, the hosted model 4.0). Measured traces of the same harness: 95.7 % prefix hit, misses re-read 3.8-5.3x the irreducible prefill
rows.unit: fresh prompt tokens per output token
rows.src: https://huggingface.co/datasets/netpreme/coding_agent_traces and https://arxiv.org/html/2606.30560v2 (fresh per output = (input / output) / (1 + cache / new))

rows.statement: Our own coding-agent CLI traffic on the vendor's hosted API (Anthropic), 1.19M requests: uncached plus cache-write prompt tokens per output token (main threads 6.2, subagents 9.1; last 7 days 8.6, of which main 4.3 and subagents 11.1). This is what a server that caches well serves for our agents
rows.unit: fresh prompt tokens per output token
rows.src: MEASURED: lab notes over our coding-agent CLI transcripts, 2026-10-26, results in lab notes (its hosted-usage section): 1,185,373 responses deduplicated by message id, the hosted vendor's models only: (input + cache_creation) / output tokens

rows.statement: The same 1.19M hosted requests counting every prompt token, cache reads included: the whole prompt is about 380 times the output (main threads 581, subagents 234), so almost every prompt token must come from a cache, never a re-read
rows.unit: prompt tokens (all, cache reads included) per output token
rows.src: MEASURED: lab notes over our coding-agent CLI transcripts, 2026-10-26, results in lab notes (its hosted-usage section): 1,185,373 responses deduplicated by message id, the hosted vendor's models only: (input + cache_creation + cache_read) / output tokens

rows.statement: The recorded trace our 16-agent replays loop (trace-r8, 9 agents, 158 turns): its cold first prompts (110,424 tokens) plus each turn's prompt growth past the previous prompt (214,508) over its recorded outputs (72,208) = 4.5. A replay that reads more fresh tokens per output than this re-read what a perfect cache keeps
rows.unit: fresh prompt tokens per output token
rows.src: MEASURED: lab notes trace trace-r8 (sha256 5e17dac21d26), every turn's rec_prompt_tokens and out_tokens; the trace as recorded on the hosted API read 6.6 uncached tokens per output

rows.statement: Truly new prompt content in coding-agent traces is about 1.5 tokens per output token (12.3 % of the hosted model's append tokens); everything above it is re-read
rows.unit: fresh prompt tokens per output token
rows.src: INFERRED from https://arxiv.org/html/2606.30560v2 Table 12: 1,154 M append and 142 M fresh tokens over about 136k steps of 690 output tokens

rows.statement: Distinct experts a batch window touches grow far slower than its rows: N (1 - (1 - k / N)^B). For 512 experts top-10: about 139 at 16 rows (32 agents in 2 groups) and 240 at 32 rows (64 agents), so expert bytes per row fall only 13 % from 32 to 64 agents and decode capacity does not double (about 420 tok/s at 64 agents, not 2 x 362). Published: 62 % of 256 experts at batch 32, 95 % at batch 64 (DeepSeek-R1); 168.6 of 256 at batch 64 (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B)
rows.src: INFERRED: the uniform formula on our model geometry (lab notes, item 4); published curves https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.07265v1.pdf and https://arxiv.org/html/2608.13962

rows.statement: Restoring an agent's parked state beats reading its prompt again by about 500x: one 100k-token agent (about 1.27 GB of KV, indexer keys and recurrent state) moves over a 56 Gb IB link in about 0.19 s, and re-reads in about 95 s at 1,050 prompt tok/s. Every eviction that turns into a re-read is the costliest event of a run; 64 agents at 100k park about 81 GB
rows.src: INFERRED: lab notes item 3; host-DRAM offload published at 3.0x lower TTFT on 32 agents x 100k https://blog.lmcache.ai/en/2026/05/12/benchmarking-lmcache-for-multi-turn-agentic-workloads-on-amd-mi300x/

rows.statement: Chunked prefill with stall-free batching (Sarathi-Serve) raises serving capacity 2.6-5.6x under a latency target; 512-token chunks cost up to about 25 % more prefill time, 2048-token chunks almost nothing

While fresh per output stays at 24, perfect prefill/decode overlap only moves useful output from min-serial 39 to min(D, P / F) = 44 tok/s at 32 agents (+13 %): chunking fixes TTFT and stalled decode first, throughput only once F falls to about 5
rows.src: INFERRED: lab notes item 2: F 24, P 1,050, D 362

rows.statement: A layer-split pipeline whose stages do not overlap inside a prompt read loses to pipeline bubbles; removing them (DejaVu: disaggregated prompt and token steps, microbatch KV swapping) gave 1.88-2x throughput
At batch 32 a speculation length of 2 or less is best; longer speculation slows batched decode
rows.unit: max draft tokens a step at batch 32

rows.statement: In an MoE a speculation length s turns a batch of B rows into B (s + 1) rows for the experts: MTP-3 at 16 rows touches about 367 of 512 experts instead of 139 (2.6x the expert bytes a window)
rows.src: INFERRED: B (s + 1) from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.07265v1.pdf on our geometry (lab notes, item 8)

rows.statement: Batched MTP on this model likely breaks even near 8 rows a window and loses at 32 and 64 agents (16 and 32 rows): keep batch MTP off there
rows.src: INFERRED: lab notes item 8: acceptance 2-2.8 tokens a step against 2.6x the expert bytes

rows.statement: The coding-agent CLI aborts a stream that receives no bytes for 5 minutes on a non-vendor provider (response headers wait up to 600 s), then resends the whole prompt. A closed loop of agents on a saturated server stretches each turn (Little's law): at about 14 turns a minute, 64 agents wait about 4.6 min a turn, at the watchdog

The coding-agent CLI compacts at its assumed window minus min(max output, 20k) minus 13k: about 167k tokens for a 200k window. A server window below that makes requests between the server limit and 167k fail instead of compacting, unless the client's auto-compact window is lowered
rows.src: INFERRED: the vendor documents auto-compaction near the window limit (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window); the exact formula is our reading of the client's behaviour, not a documented figure
